hints: Focus on what the words formation really mean, making one mole of a compound from its elements only.
Check each equation for two things, is exactly one mole of $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$ made, and are the reactants just $\text{H}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ in their normal standard states?
Use that test to rule out equations that make two moles, or start from ions or single atoms, to leave the one that fits perfectly.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definition of standard enthalpy of formation**

Remember, it is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states, all under standard conditions.

Definition:
$$1 \text{ mol compound formed from elements in standard states}$$

**Apply the one mole product rule**

Look at the product first. We must make exactly $1$ mol of $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$.

That means:
$$\text{product must be } \text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \text{ with coefficient 1}$$

**Apply the elements in standard states rule**

The reactants must be only the elements hydrogen and oxygen, in the forms they normally exist at standard conditions.

That means:
$$\text{H}_2\text{(g)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$$

**Pick the matching equation**

Only one equation makes exactly one mole of liquid water from $\text{H}_2\text{(g)}$ and $\text{O}_2\text{(g)}$. That is the standard enthalpy of formation of water.

options.A: This makes 2 moles of $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$, not 1 mole. Its enthalpy change is twice the enthalpy of formation, so it is really the enthalpy of combustion of hydrogen.
options.B: This is correct because exactly 1 mole of $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$ is formed from its elements $\text{H}_2\text{(g)}$ and $\text{O}_2\text{(g)}$ in their standard states. This matches the definition of standard enthalpy of formation exactly.
options.C: This starts from ions $\text{H}^+\text{(aq)}$ and $\text{OH}^-\text{(aq)}$, not from elements. Its enthalpy change is the standard enthalpy of neutralisation, a common trap.
options.D: This starts from gaseous atoms $\text{H(g)}$ and $\text{O(g)}$, not from the standard state elements $\text{H}_2\text{(g)}$ and $\text{O}_2\text{(g)}$. Atoms are not standard states, so this is not formation.
